title: The Art of Becoming Dangerously Self-Educated
segments: Three simple techniques. That's all it takes to become dangerously self-educated, even if you're starting from scratch. And it has nothing to do with talent. Step one, the explain it simple test. Richard Fineman, the Nobel

Prize winning physicist, lived by one rule. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet. Not you haven't read enough. You don't understand it. So, here's what you do. Take the idea you just learned.
Explain it out loud like you're teaching a 10-year-old. Listen for where you get stuck. That stuck point isn't a memory gap. It's an understanding gap. Go back, fix that one spot, and explain
it again. Even simpler. That's the whole method. And it's why some people forget a book in a week. While others can still teach it 2 years later. Step two, the lattice work move. Charlie Mer, Warren
Buffett's longtime partner, never read just to collect facts. He read to build a lattice. psychology next to physics, history next to economics, all cross-wired. A fact

sitting alone, disconnected from anything else, was useless to him. So, every time you learn something new, ask yourself one powerful question. What does this connect to that I already know? That single question
turns random information into a solid structure instead of a messy pile. Step three, the reconstruction habit.
Benjamin Franklin left school at 10. By his 20s, he was outthinking people with full university educations.
Not by reading more, but by doing this.
He'd read a great essay, set it aside, and then rewrite the entire argument from memory in his own words. Then he'd compare it to the original, not just to check what he

remembered, but to find where his logic was weaker. Every gap he found, he fixed. He wasn't storing information. He was sharpening a blade. Three techniques. Explain it simply. connect it to what you already know.

Rebuild it from memory. Do those three consistently and you stop collecting knowledge and start building it. Because self-education was never about how many books you get through. It's about how few ideas you actually let yourself skip past.
